data.title: Tesla Roadster revealed with SpaceX thrusters: 0-100km/h in less than a second, it can fly … and you still can’t have one
data.description:
Tesla showed the world how to make electric cars fun, fast and desirable.

It then tried to reinvent the ute – or pick-up truck – with the Cybertruck.

Now the tech-focussed electric car brand is showing what happens with you mix cars with rockets.

READ MORE: Tesla Cybercab in Australia: Our man Corby meets the future and comes away disturbed
READ MORE: Tesla Model 3 drops below $46,000! New entry grade undercuts BYD Seal as well as Kia EV4
READ MORE: How good would it be if this thing really happens? Longbow 895kg Speedster EV sports car hits British roads before planned 2026 deliveries
READ MORE: Best luxury EVs in Australia 2026: Premium electric cars under $100k, $150k, $250k and beyond, priced and compared

The innovative car maker is trying to reinvent the supercar, using SpaceX technology and thrusters to deliver mind-bending acceleration and slot-car-like cornering.

Just don’t expect to see one in a showroom any time soon.

The new Tesla Roadster has finally been revealed – almost nine years after Tesla first showed an early concept and started taking deposits.

Production still isn’t due to start until 2028.

Part Jetsons, part James Bond. Back to the Future and part KITT, the Roadster can drive upside down, leap over trucks and – apparently – fly (already some are questioning whether the flying stunts were real).

Even Tesla leaned into the movie references during the car’s live reveal – which was complete with the usual Tesla showmanship – with company CEO Elon Musk using Doc Brown’s famous line: “Where we’re going, you don’t need tyres.”

The famous underwater Lotus Esprit from James Bond’s The Spy Who Loved Me was also flashed up briefly on the screen.

Now, we know Tesla is up for some fairly bold claims that sometimes don’t hold water, but even if some of the stats around the Roadster are a little bit off, it’s still shaping up to be a supercar-shaming machine that leans on space tech as much as early Teslas leant on software and screens.

Check these claims:

0-96km/h: under 1.6sec (Performance), under 0.9sec (Thrust), under 0.59sec (Rocket)
Top speed: more than 370km/h (with Musk targeting more than 600km/h)
EV range: more than 480km
Downforce: up to 2G from a fan suction system
Thrust: more than 80kN

Nearly a decade late

The Roadster was first shown in November 2017 as a surprise “one more thing” at the end of the Tesla Semi (truck) reveal.

Back then Tesla promised 0-96km/h in 1.9 seconds, a top speed of more than 400km/h, 1000km of range and deliveries in 2020.

It was priced from US$200,000, with customers asked to hand over a US$50,000 deposit. Those wanting one of 1000 Founders Series cars had to pay the full US$250,000 up front.

Then the delays started. And kept going.

By 2023 Elon Musk was describing the Roadster as a “small potato situation” that wouldn’t move the needle financially.

And even this week’s reveal was almost a year later than originally planned.

Some of the original promises have also been diluted.

That 1000km range claim is now “more than 480km”, while the official top speed of “more than 370km/h” is down on the 400km/h-plus promised in 2017.

Musk, though, says the production car – the one promised for 2028 – will go much faster than that.

Tesla Roadster thrusters borrowed from SpaceX

The headline act is a thruster system developed with Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

Where tyres are limited by how much grip they can generate, the Roadster supplements them with thrusters that blast compressed air out the back of the car.

There are two carbon overwrapped pressure vessels (tanks) – the same type of tank SpaceX uses in its rockets – holding a combined 600 litres and about 250kg of ultra-high-pressure air, according to Tesla vice president of vehicle engineering Lars Moravy.

That feeds 10 nozzles around the car.

Six thrusters point down to help the car fly (more on that later).

Four rear thrusters handle acceleration, pushing air out faster than the speed of sound with more than 80kN of force. The result is a huge plume of white air – complete with the shock diamonds you’d normally see behind a rocket engine.

There’s no special propellant, either. The car refills its own air tanks.

“It literally is just going to puff itself up and be able to do these manoeuvres whenever you’d like,” Musk said.

Musk set a target of breaking the one-second barrier from 0-60mph (96km/h). A live run at the reveal recorded a claimed 0.81 seconds.

And he reckons that’s not the end of it.

“We anticipate being able to do better than that. The production car will actually do better than that,” Musk said.

“We’ll just ride the limit of don’t detach the retina of the human in the car.”

The Tesla Roadster really sucks

OK, so we’re borrowing a gag from Musk with that one.

But there’s also some truth to it.

The Roadster also uses a fan system under the car that sucks it to the road, creating up to 2G of downforce – enough to allow the car to drive upside down.

“This car really sucks,” Musk joked.

Tesla says tyres alone typically top out at around 1.26G, so the fans allow cornering at more than 2G.

There are two aero modes – high downforce and low drag – while the rear wing changes its pitch automatically depending on what the car calculates it needs.

Those active aero stunts are nothing new: McLaren has been a pioneer in using fast-adjusting wings to dial up the excitement and the pace.

But with the thrusters in there – a genuine first for a road car (if it gets approved for the road) – it’s next level.

“It looks like you’re breaking physics because the car sticks to the ground so hard,” Musk said.

“Acceleration, cornering, it’s going to crush every track record that has ever existed.”

That suction is also strong enough for the Roadster to drive upside down, as Tesla demonstrated on a ramp at the reveal.

Half the speed of sound

Tesla says the Roadster can top 370km/h (230mph).

But Musk says the production car will be “definitely much faster than that”.

How fast? “Mach 0.5, maybe a little higher.”

That’s about 617km/h – more than 100km/h faster than the quickest road cars yet built.

Musk’s target is tied to his planned attempt at Evel Knievel’s Snake River Canyon jump.

In short, they want the car to arrive at warp speed and thrust its way up and over to the other side.

Yes, the Roadster really flies

The event at SpaceX’s McGregor test site in Texas included two flight demonstrations.

The most spectacular had the Roadster rolling slowly towards a line-up of Tesla’s current models, including the Semi truck.

Then it fired its thrusters, shot into the air, flipped through 360 degrees over the top of them and landed on the other side.

Tesla calls it the “kick flip”.

“Flying cars are real,” was one of the quips during the reveal.

The thrusters also act as attitude control, allowing the car to roll and perform what Musk called “crazy gymnastics”.

“It can basically fly like a rocket,” he said. “It takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10.”

He also conceded it is “not necessarily a safety-optimised car”, and that flying it may not be “legal in all jurisdictions”.

Three versions of the Tesla Roadster

The Roadster will be offered in three configurations.

The two-seat Performance uses active aerodynamics and the suction system.

The Thrust model adds the rear acceleration thrusters.

The single-seat Rocket gets the full thruster set-up allowing it to fly – and is invitation-only and not approved for public roads.

US deposits are US$50,000 for the Performance and US$250,000 for the Thrust.

Final pricing is yet to be announced.

The cabin uses seats moulded into the chassis, with a yoke and steer-by-wire, brake-by-wire and throttle-by-wire systems.

Musk says the Roadster will long-term be the only manually driven car Tesla makes, with all others using various levels of self-driving tech.

“If you’re going to have only one manually driven car, let’s take it to the limits and way past the limits.”

Will it worry Ferrari?

The event was typical Musk theatre laced with stunts and showmanship (unlike the Cybertruck event where one of the windows shattered during a demonstration, this one seemed to go off without a hitch).

Yet beneath the bright lights, the Hot Wheels-style upside-down track and the air thrusters, there’s clearly real engineering depth – the really cool stuff leveraged from SpaceX.

Will it send Ferrari, Lamborghini, Porsche and others running? Unlikely.

But it could bring a new breed of car lover into the supercar world.

First, though, Tesla has to build it.

The company has a long record of missing production deadlines. The Semi was revealed in 2017 with production promised for 2019, but the first trucks didn’t reach customers until late 2022.

The Cybertruck was unveiled in 2019 and promised for late 2021, and deliveries didn’t start until the end of 2023 (sales have been soft since).

And the Roadster has already blown through its first delivery date by six years.

So when Musk says 2028 is “actually, for real”, don’t hold your breath.

Tesla Australia is yet to confirm local pricing or timing.

The post Tesla Roadster revealed with SpaceX thrusters: 0-100km/h in less than a second, it can fly … and you still can’t have one appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: VW Mission Efficiency Deep Dive: Here’s how Volkswagen squeezed extraordinary EV range from just 54.9kWh
data.description:
Electric car makers have increasingly turned to bigger batteries to deliver longer driving ranges, but Volkswagen’s remarkable Mission Efficiency prototype demonstrates there’s another way.

The German brand’s ultra-slippery experimental EV has recorded average energy consumption of just 6.89kWh/100km during a 1278km European road trip, despite carrying a relatively modest 54.9kWh usable battery.

For some perspective, plenty of contemporary electric cars consume somewhere in the teens of kWh/100km, while larger and heavier electric SUVs can easily venture beyond 20kWh/100km.

READ MORE: 6.48kWh/100km! Volkswagen Mission Efficiency electric car shows how frugal an EV can be in the real world
READ MORE: Global unveiling: After many teases, the VW ID. Polo has been revealed in full. Is this the best small EV in the world?
READ MORE: Volkswagen turns iconic GTI on its head: Electric ID.3 is first rear-drive GTI and the most powerful ever

Volkswagen’s answer isn’t one breakthrough technology. Instead, it has attacked virtually everything that consumes or wastes energy, from aerodynamics and tyre resistance to braking, weight, climate control and even the stereo.

And much of what sits underneath the Mission Efficiency isn’t experimental.

Its 99kW front-mounted electric motor and battery are derived from the technology developed for the new Volkswagen ID. Polo, while the underlying front-wheel-drive MEB+ architecture will underpin a new generation of relatively affordable Volkswagen EVs.

That makes the Mission Efficiency an intriguing demonstration of how much further an EV might travel if engineers concentrate on reducing its energy requirement rather than simply adding more battery.

Aerodynamics

The Mission Efficiency’s most spectacular number is its drag coefficient of just 0.158.

But drag coefficient is only part of the equation. The VW also has a small frontal area of 2.08 square metres, helped by its unusually low 1392mm overall height.

Its body then progressively narrows towards the rear in the classic aerodynamic teardrop or ‘boat-tail’ shape.

Volkswagen has attacked the airflow in less obvious places too.

The underbody is almost completely enclosed, the rear wheels are covered and three active cooling flaps in the nose remain closed when cooling air isn’t required.

The doors use frameless windows and flush handles, while the rear axle has even been narrowed compared with the ID. Polo to help clean up airflow beneath the car.

The benefits increase dramatically with speed because aerodynamic drag becomes an increasingly important component of a vehicle’s total energy requirement.

Volkswagen claims the Mission Efficiency consumes more than 30 per cent less energy than an ID. Polo once speeds exceed 80km/h.

The most telling comparison comes at German autobahn speeds: VW says driving the Mission Efficiency at about 140km/h requires roughly the same amount of energy as driving an ID. Polo at 100km/h.

Wheels

One of the more fascinating lessons from the project concerns wheels.

Volkswagen estimates they are responsible for between 25 and 30 per cent of a vehicle’s aerodynamic resistance.

So rather than simply fitting conventional aero wheel covers, its engineers worked on controlling airflow both around and through them.

The front wheelarches sit closely around the tyres to reduce turbulence, while the rear wheels are completely enclosed.

VW has also developed patented deflectors mounted on the inside of all four wheels. Their job is to prevent air entering the rims and creating turbulence. Flat external wheel covers complete the package.

Then there are the tyres themselves. Volkswagen worked with Continental to develop special tyres based on its production EcoContact 7.

Their claimed rolling resistance is just 4.9kg per tonne, around 25 per cent below the threshold required to achieve the European Union’s highest Class A tyre rating.

Battery

Mission Efficiency’s battery is particularly interesting because its capacity is nothing extraordinary. It contains 54.9kWh of usable energy – less than many mainstream EVs.

It uses NMC lithium-ion chemistry and cell-to-pack construction, eliminating conventional intermediate battery modules by integrating cells more directly into the pack.

The battery is related to the production unit developed for the ID. Polo, although Volkswagen unlocked an additional 2.9kWh of usable capacity through software for Mission Efficiency.

Maximum DC charging power is 105kW and AC charging is rated at 11kW. Those aren’t headline-grabbing charging figures. The point is that Mission Efficiency needs relatively little electricity in the first place.

Its official WLTP energy consumption is just 8.4kWh/100km. During Volkswagen’s documented 1278.36km journey from Wolfsburg in Germany to Vienna in Austria, that fell to 6.89kWh/100km excluding charging losses, or 7.51kWh/100km when those losses were included.

The battery required only one recharge during the journey and VW says the car arrived with another 164km of indicated range remaining.

A separate idealised test at a constant 68km/h, without gradients and with energy consumers such as air-conditioning switched off, produced an even lower 6.48kWh/100km.

Braking

Another potential pointer towards future production EVs is hidden in the braking system.

Mission Efficiency retains conventional hydraulic brakes at the front but uses a new electromechanical brake at the rear, developed jointly by Volkswagen and automotive technology company Aumovio.

Rather than hydraulic pressure activating the rear brakes, electrical actuators do the job. That eliminates rear hydraulic lines and brake fluid while reducing mechanical friction losses.

More importantly for an EV, Volkswagen says the system enables variable brake-force distribution and can improve the interaction between friction braking and regenerative braking.

That potentially allows more of the vehicle’s kinetic energy to be recovered and returned to the battery rather than disappearing as heat through the brakes.

Solar

There is also a 370-watt photovoltaic system integrated into the glass roof and rear section of the Mission Efficiency.

Volkswagen says it can contribute the equivalent of up to 30km of extra range per day, depending heavily on location, weather and season.

But that needs some qualification. The solar cells aren’t intended to transform Mission Efficiency into a solar-powered EV. They feed the vehicle’s electrical system and reduce the amount of energy ancillary systems need to draw from the traction battery.

It’s another example of the philosophy behind the entire car: rather than finding one enormous energy saving, VW has accumulated lots of smaller ones.

Air-conditioning

Climate control can take a significant bite out of an EV’s available energy, particularly when heating the cabin in cold conditions.

Mission Efficiency therefore uses a heat pump to reduce the electrical energy required for heating. The system uses R744 – carbon dioxide – as its refrigerant rather than a conventional synthetic refrigerant.

Volkswagen has applied the same energy-saving philosophy elsewhere inside. There’s no conventional infotainment screen. Instead, occupants bring a smartphone or tablet.

Even conventional permanently installed speakers have been deleted and replaced by a portable Bluetooth speaker.

Weight

The Mission Efficiency combines elements of the ID. Polo structure with a self-supporting aluminium construction, while the doors, bonnet, tailgate, guards and other components employ carbon-fibre and aramid composite materials.

That part of the formula is clearly less representative of an affordable production EV than its motor and battery technology, because extensive lightweight composites remain expensive.

Nevertheless, it illustrates the engineering trade-off inherent in long-range EVs.

Adding battery capacity increases range, but also adds weight. That additional weight then requires more energy to accelerate and move, potentially requiring still more battery capacity.

Mission Efficiency attacks the problem from the opposite direction.

Mirrors

There’s even an interesting lesson in something Volkswagen decided not to fit.

Despite the extreme aerodynamic focus, Mission Efficiency retains conventional exterior mirrors rather than replacing them with cameras.

Volkswagen says wind-tunnel development showed the overall aerodynamic benefit from camera mirrors would have been relatively small.

They would also have added cost and consumed electricity.

It’s a tiny detail, but one that neatly sums up the project: a technology doesn’t automatically make the car more efficient simply because it looks more advanced.

What are the implications for future VW EVs?

Don’t expect an ID. Polo with covered rear wheels, carbon-fibre body panels and a Cd of 0.158. Mission Efficiency is a technology demonstrator rather than a preview of a production model.

But its significance is that the fundamental electrical hardware isn’t exotic.

The 99kW APP290 permanent-magnet motor, battery technology and front-wheel-drive MEB+ architecture have strong links with Volkswagen’s new generation of production EVs.

Other technologies – active cooling flaps, improved underbody aerodynamics, lower-resistance tyres, smarter thermal management, reduced brake drag and better wheel aerodynamics – are far more transferable to everyday cars than Mission Efficiency’s dramatic body shape suggests.

And that’s perhaps the most important lesson from the project. The industry’s EV range battle has often focused on how many kilowatt-hours can be squeezed beneath a vehicle.

Mission Efficiency demonstrates the other side of the equation. Make an electric car require substantially fewer kilowatt-hours to travel each 100km and suddenly a relatively modest battery can take you a very long way.

The post VW Mission Efficiency Deep Dive: Here’s how Volkswagen squeezed extraordinary EV range from just 54.9kWh appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: New Lepas L6 electric SUV priced for Australia: Chery’s latest brand takes on BYD, Geely and Leapmotor from $47,990
data.description:
Chery Group’s newest brand has announced Australian pricing for its first model, the Lepas L6 battery-electric SUV, which will arrive in dealerships for test drives in early November.

Priced from $47,990 before on-road costs, the L6 enters an increasingly crowded electric SUV market where established brands and other Chinese newcomers are competing aggressively on price, equipment and driving range.

The L6 is the first Australian offering from Lepas, another Chery Group brand joining Chery itself, Omoda Jaecoo, iCaur, Freelander and Jetour in the company’s expanding local portfolio.

The five-seat electric SUV is underpinned by Chery Group’s LEXP platform and uses a 65kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, delivering a claimed 440km driving range under the WLTP testing standard.

Its single electric motor produces 160kW and 275Nm, while DC fast charging from 30 to 80 per cent is claimed to take 22 minutes using a 120kW charger.

Lepas has not yet announced an official 0-100km/h acceleration time or energy consumption figure.

Standard equipment includes 19-inch alloy wheels, a panoramic sunroof, acoustic front-door glass, a 13.2-inch infotainment touchscreen, an 8.88-inch digital instrument cluster and an eight-speaker Sony sound system.

Both wired and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connectivity are included, along with 50W wireless phone charging and automatic parking assistance.

Lepas is backing the L6 with a seven-year, unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty, an eight-year/200,000km battery warranty, seven years of roadside assistance and seven years of capped-price servicing.

As an introductory offer, premium paint will be included at no extra cost for a limited period.

Australian Lepas boss Brad Ryan said the L6 represented an important milestone for the new brand.

“The Lepas L6 BEV marks an important milestone for our brand as we introduce our distinctive approach to design, technology and electric mobility to Australian customers,” he said.

“With a $47,990 MSRP, the L6 BEV will give customers a bold option to consider in the increasingly competitive electric SUV market.”

However, the L6 faces some sharply priced opposition, including the Geely EX5 and BYD Atto 3 Evo, which both start at $41,990 before on-road costs, making them $6000 cheaper than the Lepas.

The larger Leapmotor C10 BEV is also cheaper at $45,888 before on-road costs, while the Skoda Elroq 60 Select matches the Lepas at $47,990. The MG S5 EV Essence 62 is priced at $47,990 drive-away, although that price includes on-road costs.

The L6’s 440km WLTP range will also be an important consideration against competitors offering longer driving distances between charges.

Lepas is positioning itself as a more upmarket member of the Chery Group family, but the L6’s pricing means it will have to persuade buyers that its styling, equipment and ownership package justify the premium over some established alternatives.

The L6 will eventually be joined by the smaller L4 electric SUV, although its Australian launch has reportedly slipped from December 2026 to the first half of 2027.

The L4 is expected to use the same 160kW electric motor and 65kWh battery as the L6, but offer a slightly longer 450km WLTP range. Plug-in hybrid versions of both models are also planned for Australia in 2027.

The new brand has further expansion planned, including larger L8 and L9 SUVs and an entry-level L2 hatchback.

Lepas L6 BEV – equipment and specifications

As supplied by Lepas Australia, with minor formatting changes.

Pricing

– Lepas L6 BEV: $47,990 MSRP, excluding on-road costs

Powertrain and charging

Maximum power: 160kW

Maximum torque: 275Nm

Battery capacity: 65kWh

Battery chemistry: Lithium iron phosphate (LFP)

Driving range: 440km (WLTP)

DC fast charging: 30–80 per cent in 22 minutes using a 120kW charger

Exterior

19-inch machined alloy wheels

Panoramic sunroof with retractable sunshade

Acoustic glass (front doors)

Interior and technology

13.2-inch LCD infotainment touchscreen

8.88-inch LCD instrument cluster

Apple CarPlay and Android Auto (wired and wireless)

Eight-speaker Sony sound system

50W wireless device charging

Safety and ownership

Full suite of advanced driver assistance systems

Automatic parking assist

Seven-year/unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty

Eight-year/200,000km battery warranty

Seven-year roadside assistance

Seven-year capped-price servicing

The post New Lepas L6 electric SUV priced for Australia: Chery’s latest brand takes on BYD, Geely and Leapmotor from $47,990 appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: GWM’s EV and PHEV push: Ora Touring and bigger Jolion spearhead 16-product Australian expansion
data.description:
GWM is preparing to broaden its Australian electric and plug-in hybrid line-up as it targets a 16-product portfolio by the end of 2027.

The expansion includes the Ora Touring EV, a larger Haval Jolion with expected electric and plug-in hybrid options, and a PHEV version of the Haval H7.

They will give GWM more entries in the electric family-car market, alongside its growing range of plug-in hybrid utes.

READ MORE: Toyota RAV4 plug-in has a serious rival: 320kW GWM Haval H7 PHEV to land between $50,000 and $60,000
READ MORE: Australia’s cheapest PHEV ute: GWM Cannon Hi4-T launches from $47,990 drive-away
READ MORE: 2026 GWM Ora 5 SUV Review: Sharply priced newcomer takes the EV fight to BYD Atto 2, Jaecoo J5

GWM Australia chief operating officer John Kett told EV Central the company hoped to introduce the Jolion Maxi and Ora Touring before the end of 2026.

“We’re hoping by the end of the year, we’ll have the Jolion Maxi and the Ora Touring,” Kett said.

The Jolion Maxi, also referred to as the Jolion Max, is a larger SUV than the existing Jolion, moving into the mid-size category.

Its expected powertrain choices include a 150kW/260Nm battery-electric version and a 238kW/528Nm plug-in hybrid, alongside a conventional petrol-electric hybrid producing 164kW/482Nm.

Those figures remain indicative rather than confirmed Australian specifications.

The broader powertrain selection would give GWM another contender against electric SUVs such as the Hyundai Kona Electric and MG S5 EV, while the plug-in hybrid would compete for buyers considering the BYD Sealion 5 and Sealion 6.

The Ora Touring will expand GWM’s battery-electric offering with a longer, wagon-like body, adding another option alongside the Ora 5 electric SUV.

Meanwhile, hybrid and plug-in hybrid versions of the Haval H7 are scheduled for October. The PHEV will add another GWM alternative in a family SUV market that includes the Toyota RAV4 PHEV and BYD Sealion 6.

The SUV expansion follows the introduction of the Cannon Hi4-T, giving GWM a second plug-in hybrid ute alongside the larger Cannon Alpha PHEV. Its ute rivals include the BYD Shark 6, Ford Ranger PHEV and JAC Hunter PHEV.

Kett said fresh products were central to GWM’s response to an increasingly crowded Australian market.

“I think that’s the only response to the marketplace you can deliver is new product, new interest, get people’s attention,” he said.

“There are some great performance vehicles in our 3.0-litre diesel, plug-in hybrid vehicles that we’re launching, and a couple of EVs.”

Across the combined model and powertrain rollout, GWM expects its Australian portfolio to grow from nine models to about 16 products.

“We’ll end up with a portfolio by Q4 next year that we think is about 16 products,” Kett said. “These aren’t just silhouette cars in a portfolio, they’re happening.”

The post GWM’s EV and PHEV push: Ora Touring and bigger Jolion spearhead 16-product Australian expansion appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: 450kW BMW iX3 M60 confirmed for Australia: Luxury electric SUV range gains performance flagship
data.description:
BMW has revealed the iX3 M60 xDrive, a new electric performance flagship that will top its Australian iX3 line-up when local orders open in 2027.

Announced on the same day as the related iX4 M60 xDrive coupe-style SUV, the most powerful iX3 yet combines dual-motor all-wheel drive with claimed outputs of 450kW and 875Nm.

BMW claims a 0-100km/h sprint of 3.9 seconds and a driving range of up to 754km on the WLTP test cycle, although the figures remain provisional.

READ MORE: BMW iX4 revealed: Neue Klasse electric coupe SUV confirmed for Australia from $103,900 with up to 828km range
READ MORE: BMW’s fuel cell iX5 aims for 750km range, sub-five-second 0-100km/h and sub-five-minute refuelling
READ MORE: 2026 BMW iX3 50 xDrive Review: Our first Australian test proves the hype is real! The all-new iX3 EV is a great drive with a huge real-world range.

BMW Australia lists both M60 models as available to order in 2027, but has not announced local pricing or delivery dates.

The iX3 M60 will sit above the rear-wheel drive iX3 40, priced at $89,900 before on-road costs, and the $109,900 dual-motor iX3 50 xDrive in the Australian range.

The iX3 M60 will compete with performance-focused premium electric SUVs including the Audi SQ6 e-tron and Porsche Macan GTS, while the Polestar 4 Dual motor provides another alternative, particularly to the coupe-style iX4 M60.

The Audi produces up to 380kW with launch control and claims 0-100km/h in 4.3 seconds, while the Porsche delivers up to 420kW with launch control and completes the sprint in 3.8 seconds. The 400kW Polestar also claims 3.8 seconds, putting both just ahead of the BMW’s provisional 3.9-second time.

Compared with the iX3 50 xDrive’s 345kW and 645Nm, the M60 adds 105kW and 230Nm, cutting the claimed 0-100km/h time by one second. Its maximum claimed range is 51km shorter than the 50 xDrive’s 805km.

Global orders for the iX3 M60 are scheduled to open at the end of January 2027, with production at BMW’s Debrecen plant in Hungary beginning in the northern hemisphere spring.

The M60 builds on the new iX3’s dedicated Neue Klasse electric architecture, using an upgraded rear electric motor and more powerful inverter to deliver its higher outputs. Top speed rises to an electronically limited 240km/h.

Its battery has a usable capacity of 108.7kWh, while the 800V electrical system supports DC charging at up to 400kW.

BMW claims a suitable fast charger can add up to 340km of driving range in 10 minutes under favourable conditions. The global specification also includes 22kW AC charging.

The chassis changes extend beyond the extra power, with adaptive M suspension, variable-ratio sport steering, an electronically controlled rear M Sport differential and M Sport brakes fitted as standard.

The M60 is an M Performance model, extending the regular iX3 range with additional power and chassis upgrades. The global specification includes standard 21-inch M alloy wheels, with 22-inch wheels and specially developed 21-inch sport tyres available as options.

BMW has also revised the spring and damper tuning and added front-end bracing. Dedicated M Sport and M Sport Plus driving modes adjust the drivetrain, chassis and steering responses.

The company’s ‘Heart of Joy’ computer coordinates the powertrain, braking and related driving functions, working with M-specific control software.

Exterior changes include motorsport-inspired yellow lighting elements, an illuminated kidney grille, M-specific mirrors and a rear spoiler. Availability of the yellow lights depends on the market.

Inside, the global specification includes electrically adjustable M Sport seats with massage functions and illuminated M logos, an M steering wheel with dedicated Boost and M Mode buttons, and a 13-speaker Harman Kardon audio system.

The cabin retains the Neue Klasse layout, including a 17.9-inch central touchscreen and BMW’s Panoramic Vision information display across the base of the windscreen. Australian equipment details remain to be confirmed.

The simultaneously announced iX4 M60 xDrive shares the iX3 M60’s claimed 450kW and 875Nm outputs and 3.9-second acceleration time.

However, BMW quotes a longer maximum WLTP range of 777km for the coupe-style model, using the same 108.7kWh usable battery capacity. Its claimed maximum DC charging rate is also 400kW.

The post 450kW BMW iX3 M60 confirmed for Australia: Luxury electric SUV range gains performance flagship appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Electric Tiguan revealed: Volkswagen replaces ID.4 and ID.5 with new-look SUV offering up to 600km range
data.description:
Volkswagen has revealed the ID. Tiguan, an extensively overhauled electric SUV that will replace both the ID.4 and coupe-style ID.5 globally starting in early 2027.

The five-seat newcomer brings a claimed driving range of up to 600km, towing capacity of up to two tonnes and a redesigned interior that restores physical buttons for several key functions.

However, Volkswagen Australia has yet to confirm whether or when the ID. Tiguan will reach local showrooms, with the company declining to comment to local media on future product timing or availability.

READ MORE: VW Mission Efficiency Deep Dive: Here’s how Volkswagen squeezed extraordinary EV range from just 54.9kWh
READ MORE: Volkswagen turns iconic GTI on its head: Electric ID.3 is first rear-drive GTI and the most powerful ever
READ MORE: Electric Kombi camper revealed: Volkswagen ID. California Cruise sleeps two, powers a campsite and runs its climate control for 48 hours

The reveal comes just as an updated MY27 ID.4 range arrives in Australia, bringing additional technology and driver assistance features to the model the ID. Tiguan will eventually supersede overseas.

Despite adopting the Tiguan name, the new EV will be sold alongside the existing petrol, diesel and hybrid Tiguan internationally.

It uses Volkswagen’s MEB+ electric vehicle architecture and will be built in Emden, Germany. The change continues Volkswagen’s shift towards familiar model names for its electric vehicles, following the ID. Polo and ID. Cross.

Volkswagen has produced more than 950,000 examples of the outgoing ID.4 and ID.5 combined.

Three ID. Tiguan powertrain configurations have been announced for Europe.

The entry version combines a 140kW rear-mounted electric motor with a 58kWh battery. A more powerful rear-wheel drive version pairs a 210kW motor with a 77kWh battery, while the 4MOTION all-wheel drive model produces 220kW and also uses a 77kWh battery.

Volkswagen claims a maximum WLTP range of 600km across the line-up, although the launch release does not specify the range of each version.

European towing capacities reach 1800kg for the smaller-battery model and 2000kg for versions with the 77kWh pack. Australian specifications and towing ratings remain unconfirmed.

The ID. Tiguan also gains a 32-litre front storage compartment and offers up to 534 litres of boot space.

Its exterior adopts a more upright, squared-off SUV appearance than the rounded ID.4, while conventional pull-style exterior door handles return.

Inside, Volkswagen has introduced a 10-inch digital instrument display and a 15-inch central infotainment touchscreen.

An optional 12-inch front passenger display is a first for a European Volkswagen. A privacy function prevents the driver from viewing its content, while the passenger can use paired Bluetooth headphones for audio.

The steering wheel replaces touch controls with buttons, basic climate functions move to a button bar in the centre console and a separate controller handles audio volume and track or station selection.

Volkswagen has also redesigned the driver’s window control panel.

A selectable retro instrument theme recreates the blue and red gauges of the fourth-generation Golf, with a power display taking the place of the tachometer.

The central screen can also show a personalised virtual garage featuring models including the original Golf, Golf Country, first-generation Tiguan and Beetle.

One-pedal driving is standard, while optional Connected Travel Assist adds assisted motorway lane changes and the ability to stop automatically at red traffic lights within its operating limits. However, the driver remains responsible.

Other available features include vehicle-to-load capability through a charging-port adapter, a smartphone digital key, Qi2 wireless phone charging, ventilated and massaging front seats, a panoramic sunroof and a 480-watt Harman Kardon sound system.

German orders open on October 13, with prices starting at €42,695 (almost $70,000). That pricing and the announced equipment apply to Germany, with Australian pricing and specifications yet to be announced.

Meanwhile, Volkswagen’s updated MY27 ID.4 is already available in Australian showrooms, priced from $60,990 before on-road costs for the Pro and $70,990 for the GTX.

Both receive Volkswagen’s Innovision infotainment system with a 12.9-inch touchscreen and integrated satellite navigation, along with physical steering wheel controls.

The navigation system also enables directional prompts through the ID. Light strip at the base of the windscreen.

Volkswagen lists traffic sign recognition, front cross-traffic assistance, predictive speed limiting and an enhanced surround-view camera among the MY27 driver assistance updates.

The ID.4 Pro now has an 84kWh gross battery capacity, while the GTX uses an 82kWh gross-capacity pack. Both support DC charging at up to 175kW.

data.title: Citroen reveals nostalgia-packed 2 CV Concept EV with $24,000 target price
data.description:
Citroen has revealed an electric 2 CV Concept at the Paris Motor Show, and with it confirmation the French lead the world at re-birthing its icons.

Not only is the snail-like shape reinvented for the new 2 CV, but numerous nostalgic nods turns the EV’s retro flavour up to eleven.

Round headlights (although their LED ring feels a tad tacky), vertical windscreen with exposed wipers, TPV-inspired (Très Petite Voiture) body creases, integrated air intakes, contoured door handles and black tailgate extending to the easy-replace bumper all play to the 2 CV’s heritage.

READ MORE: Radical Jaguar Type 01 revealed, and it’s confirmed for Australia with a $300,000+ sticker.
READ MORE: Legacy car brands must embrace their heritage or die. So where’s our damn Renault 5?
READ MORE: Renault’s glorious 5 hatchback EV blocked for Australia, and it’s all our kids’ fault.

The delightful 18-inch wheels also give a nod to the past; likewise old-school Michelin white font for the tyres.

Then there’s the cabin.

Colourful padded garden chair-like curved seating (they’re removable for les pique-niques), a front storage basket (also removable), soft strap door handles, single-spoke steering wheel, umbrella handle gear changer, 8-inch square ‘phygital’ touchscreen with comic book graphics and a fabric sunroof.

Not sure about the round pedals however. Hopefully the production model stays conventional.

The original 2 CV was first and briefly produced in 1939, the day before World War II broke out. Despite such terrible timing, a production version was finally made available at the 1948 Paris Motor Show, with a focus on no-frills, simplicity and cheapness.

Over five million sold up until 1990, and it helped mobilise the French masses.

Citroen hopes to do likewise but on the EV front, with this Concept seemingly close to what a production version will look like. The Stellantis-owned brand wants to have it on sale within two years, with a target price around €15,000 ($24,000).

Cheap Chinese brands are the obvious targets, but sadly, with Citroen leaving the Australian market in 2024, we’re unlikely to ever receive it.

Ah, Citroen. If only you’d have hung on! As EV sales surge, this four-door fun 2 CV delight would surely have found eager Aussie buyers seeking a look-at-me electric runabout.

The Chinese, of course, cannot pull at the heart strings by offering such heritage treats: Renault has proved with its Renault 5, Renault 4 and now Twingo that there’s huge appetite for cheap EVs that drive well and offer a familiar but reimagined design.

This same month Jaguar finally showed the result of it pivoting in the opposite manner. The troubled Brit brand’s new Type 01 electric GT (which will cost over $300,000 when it arrives in Australia) ditches Jaguar’s traditional styling cues while moving the brand substantially upmarket on price, ostracising many Jaguar enthusiasts and buyers.

Citroen meanwhile is embracing a very familiar, loved and iconic silhouette with this 2 CV Concept.

It is only 3760mm long (less than a Toyota Yaris) and actually smaller than the original 2 CV. While there’s no confirmation on battery size and motor, Citroen said it has a target weight of 1000kg. Incredibly light for an EV, but still twice the mass of the old combustion model.

It’s likely to share technology with Stellantis’ Chinese brand Leapmotor: its 4270mm B03X SUV arrives here in November, priced from $29,990 drive-away.

Spoiler alert. The Leapmotor does not look as cool as this 2 CV.

Stellantis has the largest exhibition stand at this year’s Paris Motor Show, with over 60 vehicles on display.

That includes six new concept cars for the motoring group’s FaSTLAne 2030 strategy, where it plans to launch 50 new vehicles by 2030.

data.title: Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program
data.description:
Hyundai is preparing a new generation of cheaper, faster-charging and longer-lasting batteries to underpin a massive global product offensive that will see more than 100 new or updated vehicles launched by the end of the decade.

The Korean auto giant has detailed an extensive battery development program that includes new in-house battery cells, a switch to significantly cheaper mid-nickel chemistry for upcoming EVs, smarter battery management and new technology designed to prevent thermal runaway spreading through a battery pack.

It comes as Hyundai prepares one of the largest product rollouts in its history, with more than 100 global launches and major model updates planned by 2030.

READ MORE: Revealed: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute tech will debut in Santa Fe SUV range extender
READ MORE: Hyundai Ioniq 3 priced: UK version of new EV rival for BYD and MG starts at $42,500 … that’s promising for Australia
READ MORE: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute delayed: It’s still coming to Australia but it could take until 2030 to get here

More than 18 will take Hyundai into new products or market segments and seven new vehicles are due within the next eight months alone.

The rollout will include conventional combustion-powered vehicles, hybrids, extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) and battery-electric vehicles, with electrified models targeted to account for 60 per cent of Hyundai sales by 2030, up from 23 per cent in 2025.

Hyundai is targeting 5.55 million global vehicle sales and a six per cent global market share by the end of the decade.

Central to the technology push is Hyundai’s development of its own battery cells.

The company claims its new high-performance cells can produce more than twice the output of the high-nickel cells it has previously used while reducing charging time by 40 per cent.

The first application will be Hyundai’s new EREV powertrain arriving in the first half of 2027.

That system will initially appear in the new Santa Fe EREV, which Hyundai says will offer more than 600 miles – about 965km – of total driving range.

Hyundai says the EREV requires less than half the battery capacity of a comparable battery-electric vehicle while still providing equivalent battery performance and EV driving characteristics.

The technology is also significant for Australia because EREV is emerging as a leading candidate to power Hyundai’s upcoming body-on-frame midsize ute.

But Hyundai’s battery plans extend well beyond EREVs.

One of the biggest developments for conventional battery-electric vehicles will arrive from 2027.

Hyundai says EVs launching next year will adopt mid-nickel NCM – nickel-cobalt-manganese – battery cells that will reduce battery costs by around 30 per cent compared with the technology they replace.

Importantly, Hyundai claims the cheaper cells will maintain what it describes as “optimal performance” under real-world driving conditions.

The potential significance is substantial because the battery remains one of the most expensive individual components in an electric vehicle.

A 30 per cent reduction in battery cost does not mean the price of an entire Hyundai EV will fall by 30 per cent, but reducing the cost of the pack potentially gives the company much greater scope to lower vehicle prices – or fit larger batteries and more equipment without pushing prices higher.

It should also help Hyundai compete against the rapidly expanding number of lower-cost Chinese EV manufacturers.

The first models using the new mid-nickel batteries have not been identified.

However, they will arrive during an enormous expansion of Hyundai’s electrified range.

In Europe alone Hyundai plans to cover 85 per cent of the market with a fully electrified portfolio, including five new SUVs and light-commercial vehicles, while increasing annual EV sales from 116,000 in 2025 to more than 420,000 by 2030.

Hyundai isn’t concentrating purely on the chemistry inside the battery.

Software will increasingly be used to manage the battery throughout its working life.

Hyundai says an enhanced cloud-based battery management system (BMS) will extend the average life of its EV batteries by 20 per cent by 2028.

The system will monitor battery condition and use cloud connectivity to detect abnormalities in individual cells in real time.

That could have implications beyond how long owners can keep their cars.

Battery degradation and the cost of replacing an EV battery remain important considerations for used EV buyers, while improved battery longevity potentially increases residual values and extends the useful life of an electric vehicle.

Hyundai hasn’t detailed exactly how it has calculated its claimed 20 per cent average battery-life improvement or translated it into expected kilometres or years of service.

The other major component of Hyundai’s battery strategy is safety.

Hyundai has developed what it calls Thermal Runaway Protection (TRP), designed to prevent heat from a failing battery cell spreading into adjacent cells.

Thermal runaway occurs when a battery cell experiences an uncontrolled increase in temperature that can trigger further cells, potentially creating a chain reaction within the battery pack.

Rather than simply delaying the spread of heat, Hyundai claims its TRP system can block it at the source.

It combines a battery design that dissipates heat with barriers between individual cells intended to stop heat transfer.

Hyundai says the technology has been verified through more than 200 repeated tests using both prismatic and pouch-type NCM batteries.

The cloud-based BMS and TRP effectively provide two layers of defence.

The BMS is intended to detect abnormal behaviour early enough for preventative action to be taken, while TRP provides a physical defence against heat spreading if a cell does fail.

The new thermal-runaway technology will make its production debut with Genesis, with Hyundai’s roadmap identifying the upcoming electric GV90 flagship SUV as its first application.

The battery investment is part of a broader change in Hyundai’s electrification strategy.

Rather than relying exclusively on battery-electric vehicles, Hyundai is expanding across EVs, hybrids and EREVs as it pushes towards its 5.55-million annual sales target.

Among the models identified in the latest roadmap are the IONIQ 3, new-generation Tucson and Tucson Hybrid, Santa Fe EREV, a new electric SUV for India and new global and European B-segment SUVs.

Genesis will simultaneously expand beyond pure EVs with its first hybrid, the GV80 Hybrid, as well as an EREV SUV targeting more than 640 miles – around 1030km – of total range and the battery-electric GV90 flagship.

The post Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: BMW iX4 revealed: Neue Klasse electric coupe SUV confirmed for Australia from $103,900 with up to 828km range
data.description:
BMW’s first iX4 electric coupe SUV will arrive in Australia in the first quarter of 2027, bringing up to 828km of claimed driving range and a starting price of $103,900 before on-road costs.

Two dual-motor all-wheel-drive variants will be offered initially: the iX4 40 xDrive at $103,900 and the iX4 50 xDrive at $119,900.

An M60 xDrive performance flagship will join the Australian line-up later in 2027. BMW’s global press kit lists provisional outputs of 450kW and 875Nm, a 3.9-second 0-100km/h sprint and up to 777km of WLTP range from a 108.7kWh usable battery. Australian pricing has not been announced.

READ MORE: New BMW X5 revealed: The fifth-generation luxury SUV will include an iX5 EV for the first time
READ MORE: BMW M3 EV revealed! Stunning wide-hipped concept previews 750kW production Neue Klasse electric weapon
READ MORE: The iconic BMW 3 Series goes electric! Meet the 2027 Neue Klasse BMW i3 xDrive 50

The electric iX4 slots into similar price territory to the petrol-powered X4. Against the 2025 X4 list prices, the $103,900 iX4 40 xDrive is $6200 dearer than the X4 xDrive20i M Sport but $4500 cheaper than the xDrive30i M Sport. The $119,900 iX4 50 xDrive also undercuts the petrol six-cylinder X4 M40i by $17,300. All prices exclude on-road costs.

Logical rivals for the BMW iX4 include the Audi Q6 Sportback e-tron and Polestar 4 coupe, which also combine electric power with a sloping-roof SUV body. The Porsche Macan Electric and Mercedes-Benz GLC with EQ Technology provide alternatives for buyers considering a premium electric SUV, while the forthcoming iX4 M60 will target performance models such as the Audi SQ6 Sportback e-tron and Porsche Macan 4S Electric.

The iX4 is the third model built on BMW’s dedicated Neue Klasse electric architecture, following the iX3 SUV and i3 sedan, and extends the technology into a lower-roofed coupe SUV body.

It arrives amid a broader expansion of BMW’s electric range that also includes a confirmed i3 Touring wagon and the forthcoming iX5. The larger iX5 adopts Neue Klasse technology but uses an updated version of BMW’s existing CLAR platform.

The entry-level iX4 40 xDrive produces a combined 275kW and 520Nm, with BMW claiming a 5.6-second sprint from 0-100km/h.

Its 82.6kWh usable battery delivers up to 638km of WLTP range and supports DC charging at up to 300kW.

The iX4 50 xDrive increases outputs to 345kW and 645Nm, cutting the claimed 0-100km/h time to 4.9 seconds.

A larger 108.7kWh usable battery provides up to 828km of WLTP range, while maximum DC charging power rises to 400kW.

That gives the 50 xDrive the same battery capacity, power, torque and acceleration time as the equivalent iX3, but an extra 23km of maximum claimed range compared with the upright SUV’s 805km.

BMW claims both iX4 variants can recharge from 10 to 80 per cent in 21 minutes at a suitable high-power charger. Under ideal conditions, the 50 xDrive can add up to 387km of WLTP range in 10 minutes, while the 40 xDrive can add up to 301km.

Both models use an 800-volt electrical system and BMW’s sixth-generation eDrive technology, including cylindrical battery cells. The Australian technical specification table lists 22kW AC charging for both variants.

At that rate, BMW quotes a full recharge in four hours and 15 minutes for the 40 xDrive and five hours and 30 minutes for the 50 xDrive.

The global specification also lists bidirectional charging capability, including vehicle-to-load power at up to 3.7kW and vehicle-to-home and vehicle-to-grid operation at up to 11kW. BMW Australia has not confirmed which functions will be available locally.

The quoted driving ranges are maximum WLTP figures, with BMW warning that optional larger wheels reduce range.

Measuring 4782mm long, 1895mm wide and 1595mm high, the iX4 rides on a 2897mm wheelbase and has a claimed drag coefficient of 0.23.

Its sloping roofline is accompanied by a pronounced rear spoiler and slim horizontal rear lights, while the front combines BMW’s kidney grille and headlights into a single graphic treatment.

Boot capacity is 490 litres, expanding to 1600 litres with the rear seats folded. Another 58 litres of storage is available beneath the bonnet.

The coupe body carries a practicality penalty compared with the iX3, which offers a 520-litre boot and 1750 litres with its rear seats folded.

Both launch variants are rated to tow up to 2000kg braked in European specification, although an Australian towing figure has not been confirmed in the local release.

Australian standard equipment includes an M Sport package, 20-inch alloy wheels, adaptive M suspension, M Sport brakes and a panoramic glass sunroof.

Both variants also receive electrically adjustable front seats with memory, heated front and rear seats, a heated steering wheel, Harman Kardon audio, wireless phone charging and an automatic tailgate.

The cabin adopts BMW’s Panoramic iDrive system, combining a display projected across the lower section of the windscreen with a 17.9-inch central touchscreen and a multifunction steering wheel.

A 3D head-up display is also listed as standard in the Australian equipment schedule, along with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

Driver assistance includes adaptive cruise control, steering and lane control assistance, and Parking Assistant Plus.

BMW’s “Heart of Joy” computer coordinates the drive system, braking, energy recuperation and steering-related functions. The company claims regenerative braking can handle up to 98 per cent of braking in everyday driving.

The M60 adds an electronically controlled rear locking differential and specific chassis tuning, according to the global press kit. Final Australian equipment details are yet to be announced.

Options for the launch variants include a $3500 M Sport Pro package, $4000 leather upholstery and wheels up to 22 inches. Most metallic paint finishes cost $2000, while Frozen Space Silver costs $6000.

The iX4 will be built at BMW’s Debrecen factory in Hungary.

The post BMW iX4 revealed: Neue Klasse electric coupe SUV confirmed for Australia from $103,900 with up to 828km range appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Lexus TZ confirmed for Australia: Three-row electric SUV to take on Kia EV9 and Volvo EX90 in 2027
data.description:
Toyota-owned Japanese luxury brand Lexus has confirmed its new TZ three-row electric SUV will launch in Australia in 2027, adding a larger family model to its battery-electric line-up.

The Australian commitment follows the earlier announcement of right-hand-drive production, which put the luxury SUV in contention for local sale but stopped short of confirming its arrival.

The TZ will compete with the Kia EV9 Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Volvo EX90, although Australian pricing, specifications and a more precise launch date have yet to be announced.

READ MORE: Just nine for Australia: Lexus RZ 600e performance flagship costs the same as original top-spec RZ
READ MORE: New Lexus NX confirmed for Australia: Plug-in hybrid SUV gets bigger battery, 100km-plus EV range and DC fast charging
READ MORE: New Lexus ES EV deep dive: World-first cabin tech, new operating system and safety technology that can call for help if its driver is incapacitated
READ MORE: Three-row Lexus TZ EV looking good for Australia: Kia EV9 and Volvo EX90 fighter to be built in right-hand drive

Local buyers will get an early opportunity to see the TZ at the 2026 Melbourne Cup Carnival, where it will be displayed alongside the limited-edition RZ 600e F Sport Performance at Lexus’s pavilion in the Birdcage Enclosure at Flemington Racecourse.

The TZ revealed overseas measures 5100mm long, 1990mm wide and 1705mm tall, with a 3050mm wheelbase. Its cabin has six seats arranged in three rows of two, including individual second-row seats with heating, ventilation and ottoman-style leg rests.

Previously announced overseas specifications include a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain producing 300kW, a 95.8kWh battery and a claimed driving range of up to 530km on the WLTP test cycle.

Lexus claims a 0-100km/h acceleration time of 5.4 seconds. DC charging peaks at 150kW, with a claimed 10-80 per cent recharge taking 35 minutes. Those figures have yet to be confirmed for the Australian version.

The overseas model also features rear-wheel steering, a 14.5-inch infotainment touchscreen and a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster. Boot capacity is quoted at 290 litres with all six seats in use, expanding to 2017 litres with the second and third rows folded.

Lexus Australia chief executive Jack Hobbs said the two electric SUVs would serve different roles in the brand’s range.

“The all-new TZ and RZ 600e F SPORT Performance showcase the duality of Lexus electrification. One expands luxury through space and versatility; the other pushes the boundaries of thrilling performance.”

The RZ 600e F Sport Performance is due locally in late 2026, with just nine examples allocated to Australia.

Already priced at $135,000 before on-road costs, it sits above the RZ 500e Luxury and Sports Luxury and RZ 550e F Sport in the updated electric SUV range.

The 600e combines a 77kWh battery with a 313kW dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain. Lexus claims 0-100km/h in 4.4 seconds and up to 420km of WLTP range.

Its changes include sports suspension lowered by 20mm, additional aerodynamic components, unique 21-inch wheels and a yoke-style steering wheel paired with steer-by-wire technology.

The post Lexus TZ confirmed for Australia: Three-row electric SUV to take on Kia EV9 and Volvo EX90 in 2027 appeared first on EV Central.
